<reflection>
- The second experiment successfully induced divergence among the models. The introduction of initial product and higher catalyst concentration caused product-induced deactivation models (M12, M17) and standard Michaelis-Menten (M1) to fall behind the leading pack.
- The top-fitting models are now predominantly deactivation mechanisms, specifically substrate-induced deactivation (M16, M11) and spontaneous deactivation (M14, M9, M20). My aim to break the degeneracy was achieved, and we now have a clear cluster of leading hypotheses centered around catalyst degradation.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To distinguish between the leading deactivation mechanisms, we must probe their differing dependencies on substrate and catalyst states. Currently, M16 (S + catS -> inactive), M11 (S + cat -> inactive), M14 (catS -> inactive), and M9 (cat -> inactive) are all highly plausible. 
By running an experiment at the maximum substrate concentration (S=5.0) with no initial product (P=0.0) and a moderate catalyst concentration (cat=0.1), we will saturate the catalyst, driving the equilibrium strongly toward the catalyst-substrate complex (catS) and minimizing free catalyst (cat). 
Under these conditions:
1. M16 will exhibit drastically accelerated deactivation because its rate depends on both [S] and [catS], both of which will be maximized. The reaction will likely stall early.
2. M14 will show a steady, saturated rate of deactivation proportional only to [catS] (which approximates total catalyst).
3. M9 and M11 will show significantly reduced deactivation rates because they rely on free [cat], which is depleted by the high substrate concentration.
This single extreme substrate condition will cleanly separate the S-dependent, catS-dependent, and free cat-dependent deactivation models.
</hypothesis>
